summary: Defines the INFO method for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), which lets endpoints send application-level information during an existing session, along with an Info Package mechanism for defining what such messages carry. It also keeps a legacy mode compatible with earlier use. It is a proposed standard and obsoletes RFC 2976.

eli5.summary: During a phone call you can pass little notes to each other. This sets the rules for what the notes can say and how to label them.

subtitle: SIP gets a method for passing application data inside a call, plus a labelling scheme so both ends know what the data means.

tldr.problem: RFC 2976 let SIP endpoints send application data in INFO messages, but gave no way to say which applications an endpoint accepted or which one a message belonged to. That forced static configuration and caused interoperability problems.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC redefines INFO and adds Info Packages. An endpoint lists the packages it will accept in a Recv-Info header field, and each INFO request names its single package in an Info-Package header field.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2976, keeps old-style usage working as legacy INFO usage, and requires any new usage to be defined as an Info Package.

today: RFC 6086 is a Proposed Standard and replaces RFC 2976. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it, per the metadata for this unit.

sections.title: What INFO Is For
sections.content:
RFC 6086 defines the INFO method for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP, RFC 3261). Its purpose is to carry application level information between endpoints, using the SIP dialog signaling path. INFO is not used to change the dialog or the session itself. It lets the applications that use the session exchange information, which might update the state of those applications.

INFO does not create a separate dialog usage. INFO messages are always part of, and share the fate of, an invite dialog usage (RFC 5057). They cannot be sent as part of other dialog usages or outside an existing dialog.

The RFC also defines the Info Package mechanism. An Info Package specification defines the content and meaning of the information carried in an INFO message tied to that package.
sections.eli5: Imagine two people on a phone call who also pass notes through the same messenger. INFO is the note. It only works while the call is going on.

sections.title: Why Legacy INFO Needed Fixing
sections.content:
Many applications already used INFO as defined in RFC 2976, which this RFC calls legacy INFO usage. The RFC lists ISUP and QSIG encapsulation, the MSCML and MSML media server protocols, fast video update requests, and Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency (DTMF) tones. The DTMF and video update uses were proprietary and not standardized, and the RFC notes that some legacy usages are shortcuts to more appropriate mechanisms.

RFC 2976 gave a UA no way to say in which applications it supported INFO, or which application a given message belonged to. Legacy usages therefore often needed static configuration, which caused interoperability problems in the industry.

The SIP Working Group debated for years whether to fix INFO with a registration mechanism or to deprecate it. It chose to publish a framework for registering Info Packages.
sections.eli5: Before, everybody used the note service in their own private way and had to agree on the rules beforehand. This fix gives every kind of note a label.

sections.title: Legacy Usage and Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
The RFC does not deprecate legacy INFO usage and does not force anyone to define packages for it. It sets three rules.

  • A UA MUST NOT put an Info-Package header field in a legacy INFO request.
  • Any new usage MUST use the Info Package mechanism, which can be registered with IANA.
  • A UA may enable both kinds in one invite dialog usage, but SHALL NOT mix them to carry the same application information, and SHALL prefer an Info Package when possible.

Because legacy usages have no package, Recv-Info and Info-Package cannot be used with them.
sections.eli5: The old way of passing notes is still allowed, but anything new must use the labelled way. You may not send the same note both ways.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving INFO Requests
sections.content:
An INFO request is built like any other non-target-refresh request in an existing invite dialog usage. A sender that ties the request to a package MUST include an Info-Package header field, and one request can be tied to only one package. An INFO request MUST NOT contain Recv-Info. A UA MUST NOT send INFO outside an invite dialog usage, and MUST NOT send a package's INFO unless the remote side has said it will receive that package in this dialog.

A receiver that gets INFO for a package it did not agree to accept MUST answer 469 (Bad Info Package) and list the packages it will accept in Recv-Info. That is a transaction-only failure and does not end the dialog. If the body has a MIME type the UA supports, but not for that package, the RFC recommends 415. Otherwise, a syntactically correct, well structured request gets 200 (OK). Rejecting the information itself happens at the application level, by sending a new INFO.

The package payload sits in a body part marked with Content-Disposition: Info-Package, either a single MIME type or a multipart body. UAs MUST support multipart bodies (RFC 5621). INFO responses MUST NOT carry package bodies. Proxies need no extra behavior beyond RFC 3261. There is no delivery order mechanism, but packages can use the CSeq header field to spot out-of-order requests.
sections.eli5: You may only send a kind of note if the other person said they want that kind. If you send the wrong kind, they hand it back and tell you which kinds they take. The call keeps going.

sections.title: Recv-Info and the Header Fields
sections.content:
A UA that supports the mechanism MUST use the Recv-Info header field to list the packages it will receive INFO for in a session. It may list several packages, or send an empty Recv-Info to say it wants none while still showing it supports the mechanism. A set stays valid until the UA sends a new, or empty, set. Listing INFO in Allow does not by itself signal package support.

  • The sender of an initial INVITE MUST include Recv-Info, even if empty.
  • The receiver MUST include it in a reliable 18x/2xx response, and MUST NOT include it if the request had none.
  • Unlike SDP answers, the answer set need not be a subset of the offer.
  • If the request is rejected, both sides roll back to the previous set.

There is no priority order among similar packages. The mechanism has no option-tag. A UA may put Recv-Info in REGISTER only when the package specification says how a registrar uses it. Because of forking, a caller must be ready for different Recv-Info values from different remote UAs during the early dialog.

Two header fields are added to the SIP grammar. Info-Package holds one package type and Recv-Info holds a possibly empty list. Package names are matched octet by octet, so they are case sensitive, and parameters are not compared. The RFC defines no package names itself.
sections.eli5: Before passing notes, each side tells the other which kinds of notes it likes. They can change their list later, or say they want none.

sections.title: Writing an Info Package Specification
sections.content:
A package specification MUST not weaken any SHOULD or MUST in this RFC, though it may strengthen weaker words. It MUST address, or explain why it skips, these topics:

  • an overall description and where it applies;
  • why INFO was chosen over another mechanism;
  • the package name (the mechanism has no versioning, so a name like foo_v2 is just a name);
  • any parameters, and whether they apply to Recv-Info, Info-Package or both;
  • MIME types of the body parts, and whether multipart is needed;
  • usage restrictions, such as overlapping requests;
  • any maximum or minimum request rate;
  • security needs, or a statement that none are added.

Option-tags are optional. Implementation details and demonstrative message flows are strongly recommended or recommended.

IANA created an Info Packages registry with the policy Specification Required. Each entry has a case-sensitive name and a reference, and IANA must not register two names that differ only in case. The RFC also registered the Info-Package and Recv-Info header fields, the info-package content disposition, and response code 469 (Bad Info Package).
sections.eli5: Anyone who invents a new kind of note must write down what is in it, how often it is sent, and how to keep it private. Then it goes in a public list.

sections.title: Choosing INFO Wisely
sections.content:
The RFC asks designers whether INFO is the right tool or just easy. INFO messages differ from most SIP messages because their size and rate are set by the application. There is no default throttling. The RFC says DTMF applications can generate a burst of up to 20 messages per second, and constant GPS updates could be a steady stream. Messages may cross links without congestion control. SIP messages tend to be about 500 bytes to 32K bytes, so bulk data belongs elsewhere.

Alternatives it names are SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY, the MESSAGE method, media plane channels (MRCP, MSRP) and HTTP. It points out that signaling through the SIP network can add hundreds of milliseconds of latency, so a low-latency need favors a media channel.
sections.eli5: Passing notes is fine for small, occasional messages. For big parcels or very fast chatter, use a different delivery service.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC expects the framework to help security by removing unreviewed INFO usages and letting a UAS and other security devices tie requests to packages that were negotiated for the session. Rogue UAs can still send unrelated INFO requests.

INFO may need more protection than the dialog around it. Even with SIP over TLS, any SIP hop can view, modify or intercept INFO, so private payloads need end-to-end encryption such as S/MIME. Each package must list its own requirements. Digest challenges can also be applied to INFO, for example with auth-int, if the challenger is still in the path.
sections.eli5: Notes pass through helpers along the way, and each helper could peek. If a note is private, put it in a locked envelope that only the other person can open.
